title: Example 1
headline: Six things this basket gets right
primary_text:
There is a kind of house where even the laundry basket has been thought about, and my friend Vera's is one of them. I went up to use her bathroom during coffee last week and there it was on the landing, a quilted basket in honey gold with a great bumblebee on the front and daisies growing round the bottom, standing there as smartly as a piece of furniture. I assumed it was decorative. It was full of towels.

So I came back down and asked her, plainly, why her laundry basket looked better than most of my sitting room.

It is called the Honey Daisy Bee Laundry Basket, from Manchester Boutique, a small British boutique that has been quietly dressing women our age for a few years now, and it turns out they do a whole collection of these.

Here is my confession. Everything in my house was chosen. The curtains were deliberated over. The cushions were auditioned. And the laundry basket, which I look at every single day, is a cracked plastic thing that came off a garage forecourt in about 1998 and simply never left. I had never once chosen a laundry basket. I am not sure anybody has.

So I ordered the honey one, fully expecting to send it back, and instead I ended up doing something I have never done in my life. I sat down and wrote the boutique a letter, walking through the six things this basket gets right that twenty-six years of plastic got wrong. They asked if they could put it up for other women to read, and I said yes.

The short version. It stands up on its own, even empty, instead of slumping. The artwork wraps all the way round, so there is no wrong side to turn to the wall. The handles are proper stitched ones that do not bite your fingers on the stairs. It is quilted and soft but wipes clean, and washes when it needs to. It folds flat when you want it out of the way. And it comes in three sizes, so the bathroom and the bedroom are both dealt with.

The plastic one went to the tip. I did not wave it off.

There is a sale on at the moment to make room for the autumn stock, and the collection runs to thirty designs, which is a dangerous thing to know. If your laundry basket also just turned up one day and stayed, my letter is below.

— Pat​ ​
notes: Frame B (Pat): saw it at a friend's house, asked plainly, the six-things letter. Homeware.

title: Example 2
headline: The dress four women asked me about
description: What I told them at the table
primary_text:
I almost did not post this.

I am 67 and I am not one for putting things on Facebook. But four different women asked me about this dress at Sheila's 70th on Saturday, and it started to feel a bit mean keeping it to myself.

It is from Manchester Boutique, a small British boutique that has been quietly dressing women our age for a few years now. They have their summer sale on at the moment. The dress is called the Sara. A sleeveless midi in a proper soft green, with little textured daisies running through the fabric.

I will tell you what I told them at the table.

It is the first dress I have bought in years that does not look like it was made for somebody half my age, and does not look like I have stopped trying either. That is a much narrower gap than it sounds. It skims rather than clings, which I had not realised was the thing I had been missing all along. The length means I do not think about my legs once. And it is a real colour, which after about ten years of navy and beige felt like a small act of rebellion.

I wore it to the lunch with white sandals and my good earrings, and Ann told me I looked like I had made an effort for once, which I have decided to take as a compliment. I had it on again the next morning to take the dog out, and felt completely myself.

That is the rarest sort of dress. The one you can put on for something special, or wear out with the dog first thing, and feel right in either way.

I did go and read the reviews before I ordered a second one. Just over three hundred of them, sitting at 4.2 stars. Not the suspiciously perfect five you see on some websites, which if I am honest made me trust it rather more. The same things kept coming up. One woman had written, "Ordered the green for a wedding and have worn it three times since. Does not cling anywhere and I have had compliments every time." That was the one that decided it for me.

The reason I am posting today rather than next week is that the sale is on now and the middle sizes are already going. They do it from a UK 8 to a 24, the same cut the whole way up, which I wish more places would bother with. Once the summer stock has gone it is gone until next year.

If you have spent the last few summers reaching for the same dark trousers and a loose top because nothing on the high street felt like you, this is where I would start. — Maggie ​
notes: Frame A (Maggie): four women asked at a 70th birthday lunch. Dress.

title: Example 3
headline: The outfit four women asked me about
description: What I told them at the barbecue
primary_text:
I almost did not post this.

I am 67 and I am not one for putting things on Facebook. But four different women asked me what I had on at a family barbecue on Saturday, and it started to feel a bit mean keeping it to myself.

They are from Manchester Boutique, a small British boutique that has been quietly dressing women our age for a few years now. They have their summer sale on at the moment, on a whole collection of printed dungarees and jumpsuits. Mine is a soft grey pair covered in little embroidered wildflowers.

I will tell you what I told them.

Dungarees, at my age. I know. That is exactly what I thought too, and I very nearly did not order them. But they are the easiest thing I own now. You step into them over a plain white top and you are dressed, all in one, with nothing pulling at the waist and nothing to fuss over. And the print keeps them looking like a proper outfit rather than something you would garden in, even though I do garden in them.

I wore them to the barbecue with flat sandals, and Ann told me I looked like I had made an effort for once, which I have decided to take as a compliment. I have barely had them off since, in the garden, to the shops, round to my daughter's.

That is the rarest sort of thing to find at our age. Something you can throw on without a thought that still looks like you chose it.

I did go and read the reviews before I ordered. Just over three hundred of them, sitting at 4.2 stars. Not the suspiciously perfect five you see on some websites, which if I am honest made me trust it rather more. The same things kept coming up. One woman had written, "Bought the grey pair for the garden and now I practically live in them. So easy to throw on, nothing digs in, and I have had lovely comments." That was the one that decided it for me.

The reason I am posting today rather than next week is that the sale is on now and they do them in dozens of prints, florals, stripes, even one with little bees, so the nice ones go first. Once the summer stock has gone it is gone until next year.

If you have started reaching for elasticated everything because nothing with a waistband feels good any more, but you do not want to look like you have given up, this is where I would start.

— Maggie ​
notes: Frame A (Maggie): asked at a family barbecue; 'Dungarees, at my age. I know.' Collection of prints.

title: Example 4
headline: The one bag she won't stop carrying
description: So I asked her where it was from
primary_text:
There is a woman two pitches down from us at the caravan site we go to, and every time I saw her, at the shower block, at the farm shop, walking her terrier past our awning, she had the same caramel shoulder bag on. Different cardigans, same bag. It has a wide woven strap, teal with little gold patterns worked into it, like something carried home from somewhere interesting, and it made my sensible black handbag look like a bin liner with handles.

I assumed it was expensive, some boutique thing bought on holiday abroad. Then one afternoon over the fence I asked her, plainly. And she went cagey on me. Said she liked to keep it to herself, because everyone asks. Brian told me to leave the poor woman alone. On our last morning she came over to return our mallet and took pity on me.

It is called the Tamar, from Manchester Boutique, a small British boutique that has been quietly making the ordinary things a bit lovelier for a few years now.

I will be honest about what happened next. I have wasted more money on handbags than I care to admit, a lifetime of them, stiff ones that scuffed, floppy ones that ate my keys, cheap ones that looked cheap by the second month. So I ordered the caramel fully expecting to send it back. Instead I sat down and wrote the boutique a letter, walking through the six things this one gets right that the others get wrong. They asked if they could put it up for other women to read, and I said yes.

The short version. It looks a great deal more expensive than it is, a supple vintage finish that people assume has a story behind it. The strap is the show, wide and woven and soft on the shoulder, so it never digs in and never looks like anybody else’s. It zips shut properly, right across the top. Inside it is lined and pocketed, so my glasses and keys have homes instead of hiding places. It swallows a proper day out without turning into a sack. And it goes with everything I already own.

I have since taken it to church, to the market and back to the caravan, same as the woman from two pitches down, who I now count as a friend, more or less.

I did read the reviews before ordering, over three hundred of them at 4.2 stars, which is honest rather than suspicious. They do it in black, green and cream as well, but the caramel is the one I saw first and the one I would point you at. There is a sale on now, and the first autumn stock is already going.

If your handbag is a bin liner with handles, my full letter is below, with the six things laid out plainly.

— Patricia ​
notes: Frame B (Patricia): the woman two pitches down at the caravan site went cagey. Bag.

title: Example 5
headline: The little heart bracelet she wore to the golden wedding
description: So I asked her about it
primary_text:
Two Saturdays ago Brian and I were at a golden wedding do at the social club, fifty years married, the full spread. The woman across the table from me was about my age, and every time she passed a plate along I found myself looking at her wrist. A little heart, worn silver, on a simple tan cord. Not glittery, not fussy. It looked like something with a story behind it.

I assumed it was old. The sort of piece a mother leaves you, or a first husband bought you when neither of you had a penny. But it kept catching my eye all afternoon, and by the time the cake came round I could not let it go. So I asked her, plainly. She laughed. She said her husband had given it to her, that he is not a man for grand gestures, and that this was his quiet way of making one. Then she told me where it was from, which was not a jeweller at all.

It is called the Holly, from Manchester Boutique, a small British boutique that has been quietly making the ordinary things a bit lovelier for a few years now.

I will be honest about what happened next. I have wasted more money on jewellery than I care to admit, a lifetime of it, thin chains that tangled in the box, bangles that clattered on every table, gold coloured things that stopped being gold coloured by the second month. So I ordered the Holly fully expecting to be disappointed. Instead I sat down and wrote the boutique a letter, walking through the six things this one gets right that the others get wrong. They asked if they could put it up for other women to read, and I said yes.

The short version. It is one small heart in a soft worn silver tone, matte rather than shiny, and the cord threads straight through the middle of it, so it looks found rather than bought. It means something without announcing anything, which is exactly the register a woman my age wants. There is no clasp at all, just two little sliding knots, so it eases over the hand and fits any wrist, mine included, and my fingers gave up on tiny catches some time ago. The tan cord sits lovely against every autumn colour I own. It is so light I forget it is on. And because one size fits everybody, it is the easiest present I have found in years.

I have already ordered another to put away for our eldest, because there is no size to guess and no clasp for her to fight with either.

I did read the reviews before I ordered, just over three hundred of them at 4.2 stars, which is honest rather than suspicious. One woman from Southwold had written that her husband chose it for their anniversary and that she has not taken it off since. There is a sale on now, delivery is free in the UK, and the first autumn stock is already going.

If your jewellery box is full of things you never wear, my full letter is below, with the six things laid out plainly.

— Patricia

​
notes: Frame B (Patricia): golden wedding, the heart bracelet her husband gave her. Jewellery, sends to the product page.

title: Example 6
headline: The sandals she walked the whole promenade in
description: What I told them So I asked her what they were
primary_text:
There was a woman on the promenade at Scarborough on the coach trip in June who walked the whole length of it, from the Spa to the harbour and back, in a pair of cream wedge sandals, at a pace I could not keep up with, and sat down on the bench at the end looking as if she had just got up.

Cream, one wide band across the foot, open at the toe and open at the back, and a thick soft wedge underneath, the whole foot lifted. Not a flip-flop, not a clog, not a sandal with six straps to do up. So when she sat down on my bench I asked her, plainly, what they were.

They are called the Rosamunde, from Manchester Boutique, a small British boutique that has been quietly dressing women our age for a few years now.

I had given up on sandals. Every pair I owned was either flat as a board and gave me nothing by the harbour, or it had a heel at the back and a strap round the ankle that took five minutes and a chair to do up. Forty years of it. So I ordered the cream fully expecting to send them back, and instead I ended up doing something I have never done in my life. I sat down and wrote the boutique a letter, walking through the six things this pair gets right that summer sandals get wrong. They asked if they could put it up for other women to read, and I said yes.

The short version. They slip on and the back is open, so there is no bending, no strap and no chair. The wedge lifts the whole foot, not just the heel, so there is nothing to wobble on. It is soft underfoot. The toe is wide and square and open, so nothing is pinched. The band crosses over and covers the instep, so they hold on without a single strap. And the cream goes with everything I own, and they do a black and a red, from a UK 3 to an 8 and a half.

I have since gone back for the black, the same as the woman from the promenade, who owns all three and was wearing the red the second time I saw her.

There are just over three hundred reviews sitting at 4.2 stars from women who found them before I did, and with the summer sale on, the middle sizes are already going. Once the summer stock has gone it is gone until next year.

If you have given up on sandals because they were flat as a board or took a chair to do up, my full letter is below, with the six things laid out plainly.

— Pat

​
notes: Frame B (Pat): the promenade at Scarborough on a coach trip. Sandals, sends to the product page.

title: Example 8
headline: The bag three women asked me about at the checkout
description: What I told them (in the queue)
primary_text:
I almost did not post this.

I am 67 and I am not one for putting things on Facebook. But three different women asked me about this bag during one Thursday morning shop, two of them stood behind me in the checkout queue, and it started to feel a bit mean keeping it to myself.

It is from Perth Boutique, a small Australian boutique that has been quietly dressing women our age for a few years now. They have a sale on at the moment. The bag is called the Alina. A caramel-coloured crossbody with a gently curved top, neat squared stitching across the front, and a little front pocket that sits just where your hand falls.

I will tell you what I told them in the queue.

It does the one thing I had stopped believing a handbag could do. It looks like a proper, put-together bag, and it behaves like an organised one. My phone lives in the front pocket, my purse has its own place inside, and my keys go where my keys always go, so at the till I am not the woman holding everybody up while she digs. It sits crossbody so my hands are free, and it is light enough that I forget it is there. It does not look like a bag made for somebody half my age, and it does not look like I have given up either.

I had my purse out at the till before the lady in front had finished packing, and Pauline, who I used to work with and who has never once commented on anything I carry, said it looked far too smart for a Thursday shop. I have decided to take that as a compliment. I had it on again the next morning to take the labrador across the field, and it stayed put and out of the way the whole time.

That is the rarest sort of bag. The one you can take to a lunch, or sling on to walk the dog first thing, and feel right either way.

I did go and read the reviews before I ordered. Just over three hundred of them, sitting at 4.2 stars. Not the suspiciously perfect five you see on some websites, which if I am honest made me trust it rather more. The same things kept coming up. One woman from Sydney had written, "I have stopped losing my keys. My phone finally has its own pocket and the colour goes with everything I own." That was the one that decided it for me.

The reason I am posting today rather than next week is that the sale is on now and the first autumn stock is already going. They do it in the caramel and in a black, and it is the caramel that seems to be going first.

If your own bag has spent years swallowing your glasses and your keys the moment you actually need them, this is where I would start.

— Maggie ​
